title: Sales Enablement: Enterprise Playbook — Positioning, Competitive Briefs, Pitch Deck, Pricing Guidance, Case Studies, Security FAQ
author: Maya Patel
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook equips Redwood Inference account teams and sales engineers to position our platform for enterprise prospects, respond to competitive questions, present a tailored pitch deck, outline pricing guidance, and share customer proof points and a security FAQ for technical stakeholders. Use this document as the canonical source for enterprise-facing messaging; keep decks and one-pagers synchronized with the slides linked below.

Audience: AEs, SEs, Solutions Engineers, Sales Ops, Customer Success and Partner Engineers engaging mid-market and enterprise accounts evaluating LLM inference infrastructure.

Contents (high level)
1) Key positioning and messaging
2) Buyer personas and value props by persona
3) Competitive brief (side-by-side comparisons + objection handling)
4) Pitch deck structure and slide notes
5) Pricing guidance and packaging guardrails
6) Two short case studies for enterprise use cases
7) Security & compliance FAQ for prospects
8) Next steps, owner, and collateral links

---

1) Key positioning and messaging

Leading statement: Redwood Inference is the production-first, developer-friendly inference platform that makes serving LLMs predictable, cost-efficient, and secure — across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.

Primary pillars (short):
- Production reliability: SLA-backed Dedicated capacity, predictable latency SLOs, and automated fallbacks to maintain uptime.
- Cost-aware performance: batching, KV/prefix caching, and quantization recommendations to lower $/token while preserving quality.
- Deployment flexibility: same API and operational surface across hosted, dedicated, and VPC/on-prem Private deployments.
- Developer ergonomics: simple REST/SDK, streaming, function-calling, and first-class observability.

One-liners by persona:
- Product Engineering: "Ship LLM features with predictable latency and cost so your product roadmap stays on schedule."
- Platform/Infra: "Standardize inference across teams without managing low-level GPU orchestration or custom runtimes."
- Security/Compliance: "Deploy in your VPC or on-prem and retain control of keys and audit logs while leveraging Redwood’s control plane."
- Business/Finance: "Lower per-user cost with intelligent batching and clear per-route cost analytics; predictable reserved capacity for planning."

Proof points to use in early-stage conversations:
- 99.9% uptime target for Dedicated customers (SLA dependent).
- Typical 15–40% $/token reduction from batching + cache for web-chat workloads (customer examples available).
- One-week integration for hosted API and 4–8 week timeline for Private deployments (reference architecture variance applies).

Positioning dos and don’ts (talking points)
- Do: emphasize production economics (unit cost, latency consistency, SLOs).
- Do: tailor the discussion to the buyer’s control requirement — hosted vs dedicated vs private.
- Don’t: focus only on raw model quality without discussing operational cost and risk.
- Don’t: present Redwood as a model vendor — we are a serving platform (we integrate curated open models and customer models).

---

2) Buyer personas and prioritized value props

Persona: Product Engineer (PM/ENG)
- Primary concerns: time-to-market, latency, integration overhead.
- Top value props: SDKs/REST simplicity, streaming, function-calling, structured outputs, sample prompt sets and eval harness.
- Typical objections and responses:
  - "We have an internal model." → "You can bring your model to Private or run alongside our hosted catalog; same API and rollout controls."
  - "Latency matters for UX." → "We provide per-route latency SLOs, prefix caching, and deployment choices closer to users (regions)."

Persona: Platform / Infra
- Primary concerns: cost predictability, autoscaling, capacity planning, observability.
- Top value props: Dedicated reserved pools, autoscaling policies, token-level cost breakdowns, tracing hooks.

Persona: Security & Compliance
- Primary concerns: data residency, auditability, key control.
- Top value props: Private deployment options (VPC/on-prem), KMS/HSM integrations, audit logging and retention controls, SOC2-like evidence.

Persona: Finance / Procurement
- Primary concerns: unit economics, committed spend, predictable billing.
- Top value props: Usage-based hosted tiers, reserved capacity discounts and volume tiers, clear cost attribution per product route.

---

3) Competitive brief (side-by-side + objection handling)

Competitors summarized (typical): Cloud AI managed endpoints, LLM API providers (convenience-centric vendors), and inference vendors (self-hosted runtimes).

Comparison table (high level):
| Capability | Redwood | Cloud-managed endpoints | Open runtime vendors | Model-API providers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Deployment options | Hosted / Dedicated / Private (VPC/on-prem) | Hosted-first (some dedicated options) | Self-hosted | Hosted API only |
| Production SLOs | SLA-backed Dedicated; per-route SLOs, fallbacks | Varies; typically infra-centric SLOs | Customer-run (ops burden) | Minimal SLO guarantees |
| Cost control | Batching/caching, quantization recommendations, reserved pricing | Limited unit-level tooling | High variance; depends on runbook | Fixed pricing; less control over $/token |
| Observability | Token-level cost, per-model dashboards, tracing hooks | Basic telemetry | Integrations required | Lightweight usage metrics |
| Security | Private deployments, KMS/HSM, audit logs | Varies by cloud provider | Customer managed | Varies |

Common competitive objections and rebuttals:
- Objection: "We already use X cloud endpoint; why move?" → Response: "For predictable unit economics and SLOs at scale, Redwood provides dedicated capacity and automated fallback policies that reduce outages and surprise costs."
- Objection: "We don’t want vendor lock-in." → Response: "Redwood supports open model stacks and lets you pin model versions; you can move models between hosting modes and export configs."
- Objection: "We manage our own runtime to save costs." → Response: "Operating your own runtime at scale requires sustained investment in batching, kernel tuning, and observability; Redwood amortizes that engineering work across customers while preserving model portability."

Competitive intel notes (sales tips):
- Emphasize measurable economics: prepare a short ROI calculation with tokens/day, average seq len, estimated batching gains, and reserved discounts.
- For procurement/mid-market deals, lead with dedicated POC terms and a 90-day performance evaluation clause.

---

4) Pitch deck structure and slide notes (recommended flow for enterprise)

Collateral links: canonical pitch deck (link in Confluence assets), one-pager, technical appendix. Ensure latest deck version pulled from Sales Drive before sending.

Slide flow (10–14 slides recommended):
1. Title / Customer-specific opener (logo + objective)
2. Customer challenges & why inference serving matters (latency, cost, reliability)
3. Redwood value thesis (one-liner + 4 pillars)
4. Deployment options & when to choose each (hosted/dedicated/private)
5. Architecture overview (control plane + serving runtime + caching) — include simple diagram
6. Performance & cost outcomes (benchmarks: latency percentiles, $/token ranges)
7. Security & compliance (VPC, KMS, audit logs, SOC2 evidence)
8. Operational experience (dashboards, rollouts, tracing)
9. Pilot / POC approach & timeline (milestones, success criteria)
10. Pricing approach & example TCO (hosted sample and dedicated reserved example)
11. Case study: customer X (results)
12. Implementation plan & next steps (integration checklist)
13. Team & contacts
14. Appendix: technical deep-dive, SLOs, benchmarks, model catalog notes

Slide notes: keep technical detail in appendix; main deck focuses on outcomes. For SEs: bring the technical appendix and be prepared to walk through an onboarding checklist and sample infra/permissions for Private deployments.

---

5) Pricing guidance and packaging guardrails

Pricing primitives:
- Hosted usage: per-token pricing for prompt & completion tiers, embeddings per-embedding unit.
- Dedicated: monthly reserved capacity with a throughput (tokens/sec) commitment, overage rates, and options for burst capacity.
- Private: licensing + deployment fee + optional managed support.

Decision rules for packaging:
- Use hosted for proof-of-concept and early product-market fit (low integration friction).
- Recommend Dedicated when sustained high throughput (>X tokens/sec, usually above 5–10M tokens/day depending on model mix) or when SLAs and data isolation are required.
- Use Private for regulated workloads requiring VPC/on-prem or strict key control.

Example pricing scenarios (illustrative only; use Sales Ops for final quotes):
- Hosted example: Chat workload, 25M monthly tokens → estimate $Y/month (include expected batching uplift of 25% to 35%).
- Dedicated example: 3-month reserved pool with 4 GPU-equivalent nodes for customer latency profile → committed monthly fee + per-request metering for bursts.

Discounting guidance:
- Standard discounts for year commitments: 5–12% for annual reserved contracts depending on scale.
- Strategic or proof-of-concept pricing: up to 50% introductory discounts for time-boxed pilots (with clear success criteria).
- Do not commit to deeper discounts without Sales Ops approval.

Contract & procurement tips:
- Include an initial performance SLA/acceptance criteria for Dedicated pilots.
- Include termination and data-handling language for Private deployments (data deletion, key escrow mechanics).

---

6) Enterprise case studies (short)

Case study A — FinTech customer (anonymized)\- Problem: Real-time customer support bot required sub-300ms median latency and strict PCI-adjacent controls.\- Solution: Deployed Dedicated capacity with VPC connectivity and KMS integration; enabled prefix caching and optimized batching for median sequence length 64 tokens.\- Outcome: 40% reduction in median latency compared to previous endpoint, 28% reduction in $/ticket after batching/quantization, and audit logs integrated into customer SIEM.

Case study B — Marketplace (SaaS)\- Problem: High variability in load with unpredictable spikes during marketing events; existing model hosting caused outages and cost spikes.
- Solution: Implemented mixed routing policy (dedicated baseline + hosted burst fallback) and autoscaling policies; added cost attribution per route to engineering dashboards.
- Outcome: Platform maintained 99.95% availability during peak events, capped unexpected spend with automated fallback, and reduced engineering on-call load by 60% during events.

References: full-length customer case studies and quotes available in the case studies assets folder (link in Confluence assets).

7) Security & compliance FAQ for prospects (technical copy for SEs)

Q: What deployment options help meet our data residency and sovereignty needs?
A: Use Private (VPC) deployments for cloud-hosted within regional accounts or on-prem packaging for air-gapped environments. We support customer-managed storage and can configure retention policies per contract.

Q: How are encryption keys managed?
A: We integrate with customer KMS/HSM (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, GCP KMS) for Private deployments and provide flexible key management for Dedicated customers via partner integrations. Hosted customers may use Redwood-managed keys by default or opt for a customer-managed key for higher tiers.

Q: What audit and logging capabilities exist?
A: Audit logs include control-plane events (config changes, rollouts), authentication events, and optional request-level logs (configurable to exclude PII). Logs can be shipped to customer SIEMs via secure connectors.

Q: How is customer data isolated in Dedicated and Private modes?
A: Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools and logically separated tenancy with network controls. Private installs run in the customer VPC or on-prem network under customer-administered accounts.

Q: What compliance evidence is available?
A: We provide SOC-like evidence, pen-test summaries, and a security questionnaire package for enterprise review. Detailed artifacts are shared under an NDA and via our security portal.

Q: How do you handle incident response and breach notification?
A: Redwood maintains an incident response playbook and will notify customers per contractual SLAs. For Private deployments, runbooks include customer-run remediation steps and optional co-managed response.

Q: Can we bring our own models?
A: Yes. Models can be onboarded into Private or Dedicated workflows; we support common formats and provide an onboarding checklist (model artifacts, tokenizers, config). We do not require models to be hosted with Redwood — the runtime is model-agnostic.

Security sign-off: point prospects to Security & Compliance page for detailed controls and to request an evidence package via security@redwood.example.com.

---

8) Implementation checklist / Pilot plan (recommended 8–12 week pilot)

Pilot goals: Validate latency SLOs, measure cost changes (baseline vs Redwood), and validate security integration (KMS, audit logs).

Suggested timeline:
- Week 0: Contract & NDA, scoping, PO for pilot (if required)
- Week 1: Kickoff, access provisioning, sample dataset and prompt sets exchanged
- Week 2–3: Hosted integration (or Private staging) + smoke tests
- Week 4: Performance tuning (batching, cache policies, quantization suggestions)
- Week 5–6: Load testing and SLO validation
- Week 7: Business review on metrics, success criteria
- Week 8: Decide next steps (Dedicated reserved contract, Private deployment, or continue hosted)

Success criteria examples (choose 2–3):
- 95th percentile latency under target for 7/7 days during load testing
- Unit cost reduction of at least 15% vs baseline for defined workflow
- Security controls integrated and validated via audit log ingestion
